title: To the ends of the earth (Acts 1:6–8)
hook: you shall receive power and be witnesses

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of John: three questions on the beach, by a charcoal fire. Your line was each yes becomes a job. What did you turn into action? Day five hundred thirty-four.

Some stories get a sequel. Luke's does. His Gospel finishes with Jesus blessing the disciples and being carried up into heaven. Then he writes a second volume, addressed to the same reader, someone called Theophilus, and opens it by saying, in my first book I told you what Jesus began to do and to teach. Began. Everything so far was the beginning. Today we start that second book, the Acts of the Apostles. It opens on a hill outside Jerusalem, with the disciples asking the wrong question.
screen: `A SEQUEL, PROMISED.` → `WHAT JESUS BEGAN TO DO.` → `THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.`

segments.voice: For forty days after the resurrection, Luke says, Jesus has been appearing to them and speaking about the kingdom of God. Now they ask: Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? It's an understandable question. They want to know when, and they want it to look like what they expected. Jesus doesn't argue. He says the times aren't theirs to know. And then he gives them something else, in the Douay-Rheims: "But you shall receive the power of the Holy Ghost coming upon you, and you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth." Then he's lifted up and a cloud takes him out of their sight. That one sentence is a map of the whole book. Acts starts in Jerusalem, moves out into Judea and Samaria, and ends with Paul preaching in Rome, the empire's capital. And the word to hold is witness. In Greek it's martys. A witness, in a courtroom, is someone who says what they saw. Not an expert, not a salesman, just someone who was there. In time, Christians used the same word for those who died rather than deny what they'd seen: martyr. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness. But here Jesus doesn't tell them to die. He tells them who they'll be: people whose lives tell what they've seen. Not you shall do witnessing, but you shall be witnesses. It's a description, not a task list.
screen: `WILL YOU RESTORE THE KINGDOM NOW?` · `JERUSALEM TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.` · `MARTYS: ONE WHO SAW.` · `NOT DO WITNESSING: BE WITNESSES.` · then, large: `WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about what your life shows. Sit and breathe. Picture yourself from the outside, the way a coworker or a neighbor or a kid sees you on an ordinary day. What would they say you care about, just from watching? Not from what you say. From what you do. No judging, just noticing. Then pick one small thing you'd like them to see today: patience in a line, honesty about a mistake, a kindness. If you pray, you can hold the line, you shall be witnesses unto me. If you don't, just hold the picture. The bell holds the time.
Witness. In Greek, martys: someone who tells what they saw, and later, someone who gave their life for it. Today's word.
Your line: you shall be witnesses. Today, be a quiet witness: let your one small thing be seen, without saying a word about it. Day five hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Acts 1:1–11 on the Solemnity of the Ascension, forty days after Easter (moved to the following Sunday in many places), and Acts is read at weekday and Sunday Masses through the Easter season.

fork.setup: you're with the risen Jesus on a hill outside Jerusalem. you ask when the kingdom will be restored. what does he give you instead of a date?
options: the promise of power to be his witnesses.
fork.reveal: you shall receive the power of the Holy Ghost, and you shall be witnesses, even to the uttermost part of the earth.

original.note: Greek: witnesses (Acts 1:8), from martys, the root of martyr.

trapdoor: what you thought: a witness is someone who talks about God a lot.
what it means: someone who tells, and lives, what they've seen; Jesus says they shall be witnesses, not do witnessing.
what a scholar hears: Acts and Luke share an author and an addressee, Theophilus; martys shifted to mean martyr in early Christian usage; CCC 2473 calls martyrdom the supreme witness.
